analysis.one_liner: Eliminates the federal prevailing-wage floor for construction workers on government projects.
analysis.headline: The bill to repeal Davis-Bacon prevailing-wage rules died in committee without a hearing or a vote, so the wage floor for construction workers on federal projects stayed in place.
analysis.plain_summary: The Davis-Bacon Act requires contractors on federally funded construction jobs to pay workers the local 'prevailing' wage, which is usually the union-scale rate. This bill would wipe out those wage requirements 30 days after enactment. It was referred to the Senate labor committee and never went anywhere.
analysis.who_benefits: Federal construction contractors, who could lower their labor costs by paying less than the prevailing wage on federally funded projects. Supporters of repeal also argue taxpayers would save through lower bids.

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals subchapter IV of chapter 31 of title 40, U.S. Code, the section containing the Davis-Bacon Act's wage requirements, and voids any reference to those requirements in other laws. [S2]
It takes effect 30 days after enactment but leaves untouched any existing contracts or bids already outstanding at that point. [S2]

Contractors bidding on federally funded construction could then pay below the prevailing local wage, cutting their labor costs. (General knowledge: Davis-Bacon sets that wage floor on covered federal contracts.)

analysis.who_pays: Construction workers on federally funded projects, whose pay floor would disappear; unions argue projects would then attract lower-skilled crews and undercut local standards.

drawbacks.text: Repealing the wage floor would let contractors cut workers' pay on federally funded construction; workers doing the same work on a federal job could earn substantially less than on a private job down the road.

Good-faith objection from supporters of repeal: Davis-Bacon prevailing-wage determinations are slow, paperwork-heavy, and can inflate federal construction costs, so taxpayers may overpay for roads and buildings. Repeal backers hoped lower bids would offset the wage cuts. The counterargument is that savings, if any, come directly out of construction workers' paychecks.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main effect would be a pay cut for construction workers on federally funded jobs, with uncertain savings for taxpayers. The cost is direct and falls on a specific group of workers; the benefit is speculative and depends on contractors passing savings through. On balance the bill's costs outweigh its benefits for working people.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate labor committee, which never gave it a hearing or a vote, and the Congress ended without any further action.

narrative.text: Sen. Mike Lee introduced the bill on March 14, 2024, with three Republican cosponsors. [S1] [S3] [S4]
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee on the day of introduction; that was the last action of record. [S4]
The bill repeals the Davis-Bacon Act's wage requirements by striking subchapter IV of chapter 31 of title 40, U.S. Code. [S2]
The 118th Congress ended January 3, 2025 without the bill ever leaving committee. (General knowledge: the Congress concluded on that date.)

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Construction workers, especially union-scale crews, who keep the prevailing-wage floor on federally funded projects; contractors hoping to cut labor costs lost the chance.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Construction workers keeping the wage floor

for.name: Mike Lee
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill to repeal the Davis-Bacon wage requirements. [S1] [S2]

for.name: Ted Budd, Ted Cruz, and Rick Scott
for.role: U.S. Senators from North Carolina, Texas, and Florida

against.name: Bernie Sanders
against.role: Chair, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never scheduled a hearing or vote on the bill, so it never advanced.

sides.party_line_note: All four sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat or Independent signed on, and the committee that buried it was chaired by an Independent aligned with Democrats.

industries.note: Repeal would let them pay less than the prevailing wage on federally funded jobs, cutting labor costs at the direct expense of their workers' paychecks.
Unions rely on prevailing-wage rules to keep federal work at union-scale rates; repeal would let nonunion crews underbid them by cutting pay.
Their pay floor on federal projects would disappear, though they are workers rather than an industry in the usual sense.
